Many of my clients are international professionals, and they all tell me the same thing. In meetings, they understand every word, but they do not understand the sentence. Someone says, let's touch base next week, or it's back to the drawing board, and they get lost. The reason is simple: the meaning of an idiom is not in the words. If you translate it word by word, it does not work. So here is how I teach them. Do not learn idioms from a list. Learn them in context. When you hear one in a meeting or a podcast, write down the whole sentence, and who said it, and why. After a few weeks, you will start to use them naturally. And one warning: do not use too many. One or two idioms in a meeting sound natural and confident. Ten idioms in five minutes sound strange, like you are reading from a book.

In my first year in London, I worked for a coffee trader near the river. One evening, after a long meeting, my manager looked at the clock and said, okay, let's call it a day. I did not understand. I thought he wanted to give the day a name, or maybe end the whole project. I was really worried. The next morning, everybody was back at work, and a colleague laughed and explained it to me. It just meant: let's stop working for today. That night, I started a notebook. Every time I heard an expression in a meeting, I wrote down the whole sentence. I have been keeping that notebook for six years now, and I have been adding new expressions since my first week. Today I use some of them myself, and nobody in the office thinks about where I am from.

Our first plan was too expensive, so we went back to the drawing board. Since then, we have been testing a simpler system with ten farms.
